utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is case number IT-98-29-PT, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the appearances, please. The Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Your Honour. The Prosecutor's Office is represented this morning by myself, Michael Blaxill, with my colleagues Mr. Stefan Waespi and my case manager Ms. Edel Guzman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, good morning. The Defence for General Galic is represented by Mara Pilipovic, attorney at law, here present. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. We are here today to take stock of the situation with respect to the pre-trial preparations for this case. As you know, in accordance with the Scheduling Order of the 26th of April, today's hearing will be devoted to a Status Conference convened in accordance with the application of Article 65 bis of the Rules, with a view to review the progress made in preparing the case. We will also discuss the motion of the Prosecution with a view to the Chamber travelling to Sarajevo, and perhaps we should begin with that. But as we always discuss that matter in private session, I request that we go into private session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session. I wish to address other questions with you. For today's Status Conference, I'm fully aware that this is a Status Conference intended to open up fresh prospects for our future work, and I think that in my opinion, that is, my opinion and the opinion of the Chamber, that we should keep to our goal of completing the pre-trial phase by July. You are well aware for how long General Galic has been in detention, and this Chamber will not accept for things to be prolonged indefinitely. It is precisely for this reason that I wanted to see the parties today. We are really going to take steps to complete the pre-trial preparations, and I'm telling you this to say that we really do have to finish. I think that the parties are well aware of this, and when Ms. Pilipovic took over the case, she was well aware of where we stood. We cannot allow this situation to continue. I suggested last time that we prepare a plan of work because I understood the position of the Defence, which cannot work with this enormity of issues simultaneously, and that is why I suggested to you that we take up the work that had already been done by the Prosecution, which was more or less organised previously, so that the Defence can -- should participate as we proceed with the preparations today. And with that goal in mind, I should like to tell you something else. The suggestion that I made at the last conference, and which you accepted, to work with the legal officer of the Chamber, I am going to tell you that tomorrow this is going to be a Rule of our Rules of Procedure. I know, however, that the results have not been the results we had expected, and therefore for today I should like to address again the question of the points of disagreement. I must say that the parties accepted the plan of work that I suggested, and that the entire pre-trial was divided into three stages, the first being the nature of the indictment, the facts of law and facts that were in dispute; the presentation of testimony; and the third, all the documents. The parties, it seemed to me, had accepted this suggestion. I had suggested that the parties get together that very day to make a timetable of their own. I still have no such timetable, and I intend to make one. Unless the parties prepare a timetable, I will do it. The Scheduling Order for this Status Conference already said that in May, we would address the question of witnesses, and in June, the exhibits, which means that this month we must, indeed, deal with both of these issues. In this light, I should like to give the floor to the parties for them to tell me what were the results of their meetings, how many meetings the parties had since the last Status Conference, and where we stand with respect to the totality of what I called the first stage of the preparations, that is, the nature of the Prosecution's case, the agreements and disagreements of the parties on law and fact. So as these are three matters that we need to address: meetings at the time of the last Status Conference, other meetings, and the results of those meetings, so let us hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes. During that week, which I understand was the week of the 15th of March, when there was the last Status Conference, Your Honour, in fact there were meetings between Mr. Ierace and others of us from time to time on a daily basis with Ms. Pilipovic in pursuance of the objectives that Your Honour had discussed during that Status Conference. Ms. Pilipovic did express her concerns to us, obviously, as to the resources she has and the amount of work required to master materials, but also indicated at that time certain areas where we were approaching potential agreement or not, firstly, again, in respect of the travel issue that has already been aired this morning; secondly, in respect of the issues of the stipulations, if I can use that expression, that we had submitted, matters of fact for agreement or disagreement; a considerable schedule of 90, 100 or more facts which we had set forth originally for Ms. Pilipovic's predecessor in the case. She has already made an initial comment to us on the first 13 which she could answer from the materials she held at the outset, and in respect of a meeting we had this morning, has indicated that we will be able to deal with that in its entirety by the end of this month, early June, when she would next be available for about a week to be here in The Hague and meet with us on a regular, daily basis, as I understand it. As regards the other potential meetings, I think we have had a couple towards the end of March, the last of which was, I think, the 26th. I'm so sorry, April, we had meetings at the end of April. Again, we made some progress. There was an issue that had been raised regarding potential witnesses that might be called by both parties. It was causing some concern. A memorandum agreeing on a procedure for that has been signed. We have no dispute there, and we can make progress. In turn, the Prosecution, we are -- we have invited our learned friend to consider, as it were, a breakdown of areas of witnesses so that as she addresses that block, she would then be able to discuss that with us, and then hopefully we can get agreements and/or disagreements on manageable chunks of witness evidence. That is a priority. As a result, we are in fact breaking up the witness list and breaking things into the components, and we're also breaking them down into components along the lines indicated by Your Honour, that at the end of the day you didn't want a simple alphabetical 65 ter list, you wanted something that had the witnesses grouped and would give some meaning and understanding to the witness list. So we are actively working daily on that objective. That is our prime objective at the moment. Any other issues are, in fact, being put back into second or third place, very much to reflect what Your Honour said last time. This is the order we want to go. Witnesses first, then how we present all this stuff, and then at the end of the day, you know, the exhibits to follow. In the meantime, we are creating, and have been all the while, creating an equivalent exhibit list, and clearly with the ongoing searches, of which I made Your Honour aware in the past, that these big projects have been ongoing, and we are not masters of that. We just receive the relevant information from them. You know, we have been duly adding, amending, and preparing, and we have served as broadly as we can under Rule 66(B) to Ms. Pilipovic, you heard from her. She has received some considerable amount of material, but we have tried to do so within the categories that she herself communicated so that we do not bombard her with just so much documentation that she would sink. I do, however, sympathise with the fact that there is a lot of material in this case, Your Honour, and we can't get away from that. And I sympathise with the fact that clearly in terms of her own resources, there are limitations on my learned friend in terms of personnel and, you know, what she can actually physically do and the size of team with which she can do it. So we do sympathise with that position. However, it is hoped from even our last meeting this very morning before we came in here, we have agreed on a date to, as I say, to go through all the potential facts which we have put forward for potential stipulation to be agreed, and of course, that, in turn, would shorten the evidence if that goes before the Court. Certainly we will be able to polarise areas of disagreement, and I think once, as it were, one cracks that position, that might, in turn, have a domino effect as to legal issues. So there is progress being made, Your Honour. I know it's not immediately apparent to you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask counsel to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: It's not apparent to you, I appreciate that, but I can assure you it is happening. And there is a developing, and has been a developing, working relationship where we're trying to achieve these objectives as soon as we possibly can and in the knowledge of my learned friend's resources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Blaxill, let me ask you a question. The objective that we are talking about, that is, to finish the pre-trial phase by July, does that sound reasonable to you, workable, possible, or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I stand to be corrected by others, but my own assessment would be, in all honesty, I don't think so. I think what we can do is perhaps aim for such things as deadlines because that is always a healthy pressure to keep people focussed. I think if we are looking at the reality of being totally trial ready, having completed all the searches that are ongoing in the building to honour our commitments under the various rules for disclosure, and to afford my learned friend time to prepare herself properly and present the Defence as she wishes, it is my honest belief that we could not put a line under July and say, "We are now ready and we can go completely." Of course, we could start if that were the case, but it's my understanding that the last indication from Chambers was that the trial itself would commence in January. Now, I would not advocate that we relax and put our feet up and say, "Fine, that's a long way off." It not a long way off and time passes very quickly. And certainly we are going to make every endeavour to complete our part of these things within the kind of parameters Your Honour has been indicating; however, I think it's true to say that many of the other issues depend on resolving the first issues. If we can press fast to try and reach the areas of, principally, disagreement, and then the areas of agreement, I think we then are in a position to tailor the evidence and say how can we use Rule 92 bis, how can we use video conferencing, how can we make these things work efficiently. But until we know those areas, I think it's impossible to make those logistic decisions. I simply feel that Ms. Pilipovic has recently received a lot more material. She will need some time, Your Honour. We are in May. July does seem a very tight deadline. But having said that, if we could just keep it as a spur rather than as an absolute deadline, I think we will all do our very best to work as fast as possible towards it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see, Mr. Blaxill. You know that it was my idea to have a logical sequence in terms of Status Conferences, and that logical sequence has an impact on the methodological developments. I suggested a plan of work to you last time, and I told you that it made no sense to speak about witnesses and exhibits if we do not agree on the points of disagreement. So the first issue, in my opinion, that needs to be addressed and resolved is to see what the points of disagreement are and, of course, what the points of agreement are. So in my view, that issue is a priority. Bearing that in mind, I should like to hear your views regarding the correct or adequate methodology in order to reach that agreement on disagreement. When I speak about points of disagreement, that, I think, is the most important thing for us, that is, that we should have an agreement on points of disagreement, because that will, of course, streamline the trial itself. So what are the measures, the steps that you think might be taken in order to reach that goal, in order to reach an agreement on disagreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Well, I think, Your Honour, we have two essential vehicles here. The first clearly is the indictment. That is what we have to prove and what the Defence have to answer, so I think that in itself is something where we could go through and agree or disagree specific portions. Now, that immediately tells us as the Prosecutors how much evidence we do or do not need to prove the given points that are contained in that part. The second thing would be, in my submission, that we do have the vehicle, as Your Honour suggested and asked us to do, we have the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution, albeit as a provisional document in draft, but it is a vehicle we can use. It sets out basically the legal theories and some of the factual allegations that we propose to use and rely upon in our case. I think if my learned friend can look at those two in particular, and the Rule 66(A)(2) disclosure by way of witness statements, I think that has to be the core of the case. I'm very old fashioned and assume that, you know, the best evidence is the word of mouth of the witness of fact, and then everything else is packed in around. I think if we can work from that basis, we should be able to isolate the most important thing, which are the areas of dispute, probably. From that point forward, we can then use the way that we are presenting the witnesses and will assist Ms. Pilipovic as much as we can with that so that she knows which witnesses seek to prove individual areas of the indictment and the various elements of the offences, and I think, with that, we should have a firm basis to consider the issues that remain between us. Documentary evidence, of course, often is very much supportive but can, in such cases as this, be conclusive proof in various areas, so obviously we can't look at the witnesses in isolation and we need to follow that up with, you know, the exhibits that are -- or at least the categories of exhibits so that people can turn their minds to the issues. And I think that using that progress through the materials probably would achieve our objectives fastest. Others may well disagree with me, Your Honour, but that is my personal opinion. I just hope that my learned trial lead is not the one who disagrees most. Your Honour I think that is, in essence, it. And of course, in order for my learned friend to suggest that by the end of this month/early next she will deal in whole with the facts stipulated, I'm taking that as an indication she will have been able to master sufficient of the material in order to do that, and I think therefore it's a realistic way to go about it. Clearly my learned friend has the right to approach the materials as she sees fit. I think that's the way -- in a sense, the way forward, and then the logic that you've applied I can't quibble with, Your Honour. You know, witnesses first, documents -- you know, the presentation of testimony, and then what are we doing by way of exhibits. I think that's a logical way to address it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Blaxill. Ms. Pilipovic, what is your opinion of the issues that have just been raised; that is, what do you think of the steps that need to be taken after the month of March? What do you think -- how to best achieve the goal that we have mentioned, and what is your perspective on the issue? I should also like to hear you on the issue of your Defence team, and also on pre-trial motions and pre-trial briefs of the Prosecution, Ms. Pilipovic. Can you tell us something about that so that we can try to move on with this case. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as my learned colleague has just indicated, my first task would be to make myself familiar with the material that I have just received. But notwithstanding that material, I can go on working on the facts that have been discussed by myself and my colleagues from the Prosecution. We have managed to draft a work plan regarding the issues not in dispute. Next week I will inform my colleagues from the Prosecution in writing about the position of the Defence regarding the facts not in dispute, and I hope I will soon receive their reply. We also agreed that we should meet once again at the end of May, beginning of June, to see what the situation is. And after that meeting, we would inform you in writing about the progress that has been made in respect of points of agreement and disagreement. Any other suggestion that I might make, that is -- that was my plan as regards facts. As regards the indictment and all other materials suggested by my colleague, I will be able to discuss them only once I have reviewed the documents that I have received. I shall do my best. I will make every possible effort to do that, but in view of the extent of the material, I will probably apply to the registry to be given another assistant or co-counsel so that we can adequately prepare ourselves for a fair trial that General Galic expects. So my problem is the fact that I have to become familiar with the material. A month ago we reached an agreement as to how we should work with witnesses. We did have some difficulties in that area, both myself and my colleagues from the Prosecution, bearing in mind your decision of the 5th of June. We agreed that the decision should be altered in a certain extent regarding 12 witnesses which were disclosed in the material that has been given to the Defence by the Prosecution. In order for us to be able to proceed, the Defence believes that it would be advisable, both for the Prosecution and the Defence, to be enabled to have contact with all of the witnesses who have been disclosed in the material belonging to the Prosecution and the Defence without any obligation of the parties to inform each other as to when and how they intend to work with witnesses. One of the problems that we had in terms of working with witnesses, and I think that applies both to myself and the Prosecution, is the Defence -- is the decision which prevented the Defence from working with witnesses because it was not clear to us whether potential witnesses would be the witnesses of the Prosecution, that is, the witnesses that have been disclosed in the material which has been given to the Defence by the Prosecution. All witnesses by their nature who are mentioned in that document would be actually witnesses of the Defence, but we managed to do some -- to accomplish some work in that area so far. So as regards to this month's work plan, I can just inform you that my learned colleagues and myself have agreed to continue working on the factual issues. I have enough material. As regards the first 13 facts, I have already given my opinion to the Prosecutor, and I expect their answer, and after that, we will continue working on the issues of -- issues in dispute, and we will inform the Judges thereon. I managed to review 28 maps in the past several days, and I think that that material will be very important for our expert witness. And as regards the issue of expert witnesses, we have been granted only 100 hours from the registry to do that. I do not wish that to constitute another difficulty in terms of Defence's ability to prepare themselves adequately for the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pilipovic, let me go back for a moment. During the last Status Conference we discussed the work plan that I suggested to you, that is, that first of all we should have agreements or disagreements on points of law and fact, thereby defining the case of the Prosecution; and in view of the results of such negotiations, we would then move on to the various forms of presenting the evidence and the testimonies, and then the documents. I also suggested to you that you should avail yourselves of the role of the legal officer in this work. What we now manage to accomplish with your agreement will one day become a rule. I wanted to see whether you would agree to that proposed work plan or not because the objective is also to facilitate your part of the work. As you know, General Galic has the right to a fair and expeditious trial, but it is also in the interests of the Tribunal to move on. The Tribunal will not accept a status quo, an indefinite number of Status Conferences. I have not made any calculations, but I think that we have had a huge number of Status Conferences in this case. I am aware of the fact that the Defence counsel has been changed, and we are aware of the difficulties that you are facing, but we are really trying to find the best possible work plan so that we can achieve results. And the main objective, of course, is to complete the pre-trial phase of the proceedings. If the trial is going to start in January or not, that's not something that would interest me at this point. What I should like to see done is the pre-trial phase. We have to finish the preparation of the trial. If we do not prepare the trial adequately, we will never be able to proceed with the trial itself. So I should like to hear you on the work plan, and also I should like to hear you on the use of pre-trial brief which we have to a certain extent tried to use, although it is in the draft form, but I still think that it is a usable document and that we can take it as a starting point. What is your view of that, Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to mention a fact that I don't think is in dispute here. In principle, I have accepted your work plan, but it was in the month of March, on the 26th of March. At that time I was informed by my learned colleagues that by the 6th of April, I would be given the material which was indispensable for myself in terms of preparations. The essence of my plan at that time, and the fact that -- the reason why I accepted that work plan, was that I would receive the material by the 6th of April, and that I would be able to acquaint myself with that material and proceed with the work. However, I must tell you that I only received that material, but I haven't had the time to look at it. I, practically speaking, am not aware of the contents of that material. That material is not going to be used only by myself. My learned colleagues have informed me that they intend to use that material during the proceedings. At this point, Your Honour, I am making all possible effort in order to speed up the preparatory phase of the trial, and I am aware of the fact that General Galic has the right to an expeditious trial, but he also has the right to a fair trial. The reason for which I haven't been able for the past month to proceed adequately was simply the fact that I did not have the material, the relevant material. The material that I received by my learned colleagues was just a small portion of the material that I needed. So far, as I told you, I have received 33 videotapes and about 1.000 documents. In order for me to be efficient, I have to review the relevant material with General Galic so that he can acquaint himself with the material that is going to be used. In order to move forward in this case, I suggested a plan with which my colleagues have agreed, that is, that we should deal with the issue of stipulations during this month and that we should be able to make 100 stipulations by the end of May, once again, bearing in mind the fact that I have received 1.000 pages of documents. And let me emphasise once again, that material was supposed to be disclosed to me by the 6th of April, and that was the reason why at that point in time I said that I would use the month of March and the month of April to work on that material. However, I haven't had the opportunity to review the material yet, and that is why my plan, my work plan for this month, that is, to review this documents, is simply not going to work. I will probably need more than two months, but of course I will do my best to review as much as possible and to prepare myself for the stipulations which constitute the basis for our common work in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't need any more documents, Ms. Pilipovic. I believe that you already have enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is my assessment, Your Honour, that I have 33 videotapes - that is, that one tape is three hours long - and I have 423 documents in one binder. Especially in view of the fact that those documents have been invoked in terms of Rule 70, that is, that they could not disclose them beforehand, but however, we managed to agree that those documents would be disclosed to me, and the documents were given approval by the United Nations, so eventually they were presented to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pilipovic, I'm sorry to interrupt you. As regards the issue of stipulations, I think it is something that needs to be discussed in another meeting. As you know, the rules enable us to have meetings in chambers, in my office, and perhaps we should use that opportunity. But just a very practical suggestion: You can read the indictment once again and see if there is anything that you can agree upon. Of course, you can state your position as to the issues you dispute. This is still a very general phase of the proceedings. We're not discussing issues, detailed issues. We can perhaps try and apply this very simple method: Have a look at the indictment, read it once again, have a meeting with the Prosecution and try to find out if there are points of dispute and non-dispute, and if there are points which are only partially disputed or not. It is not up to me to do your work, Ms. Pilipovic, but I have to tell you that there is a preparatory phase of the trial, of the proceedings. That is something that we have do before trial opens. I will now give the floor to Mr. Blaxill so that he can inform us of his view of the issues that have been raised by Ms. Pilipovic, in particular, whether the Prosecutor has already -- I think we're talking about documents that were submitted in support of the indictment, so whether those documents have been disclosed to the Defence, what the situation is, and also what your view is regarding the issues that have been brought up by Ms. Pilipovic, in particular, regarding the decision of the 5th of June and the issue of contact with witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: To take Your Honour's first point: Of course the supporting materials were served shortly after the arrest of General Galic as part of our Rule 66(A)(1) obligations, so the documents that directly supported the indictment were duly served at that time. Subsequent to that, and I regret my memory doesn't allow me to recall the dates, but it was only some weeks after that the flow to Mr. Kostic began of the 66(A)(2) materials, which were all the witness statements relative to the counts in the indictment and, indeed, some of the background issues and elements in the indictment. It is -- therefore, a lot of that material was in hand but, of course, did not come into the possession of Ms. Pilipovic until the end of last year when she took over from Mr. Kostic. Now I understand that she had received all of that material by the end of the year or early this year from him. Subsequently, indeed there has been further disclosure as a result, in part, of the ongoing searches, and yes, indeed, a considerable amount of material has been forwarded to her. But I think as to the general nature of the materials in support of the indictment, that it's not a voluminous amount, and it's certainly something upon which Ms. Pilipovic can work. But of course, it's greatly expanded by subsequent disclosure. Thus, as regards going forward to stipulations, yes, I mentioned it earlier, I'd be more than happy if Ms. Pilipovic wanted to go through the indictment and just use a red pen and a blue pen for what she thinks she agrees and disagrees, and that would give us any indication of where to go; and likewise, anything in the pre-trial brief that she would care to highlight as areas of dispute or agreement, again, I think that would help us where to go. And that would tailor, in a way, also the presentation of the evidence because we could -- in negotiating a point in dispute at that initial stage, we would, of course, draw attention to relevant evidence, and then we could see whether or not that issue remained an issue or was agreed. So I'm quite happy that we should proceed on that basis. Other than that, I think the June 5th decision -- essentially, I think, we've resolved our issue. A memorandum has been signed by Ms. Pilipovic, and independently signed by Mr. Ierace, and it is in fact something we can now file that informs the Chamber that we have resolved the issue regarding those witnesses. Essentially, there are 12 witnesses contained in a letter of the 19th of January this year from the Defence to the Prosecution. And we found at that time certain of these people had been interviewed by the Prosecution and we had an intention of interviewing others of them. As a result, what we have basically agreed, and I don't think it will cause any problem to the Chamber, is as follows: The parties are agreed that each side may interview or continue to interview any or all of the 12 persons without a representative of the other side being present. And further, the parties understand this agreement does not affect the Rules of Evidence and Procedure as to who, if any, of the 12 persons the Prosecution or Defence call as a witness. So I think it's an example of an agreement, Your Honour. I don't think it causes any further problems. So that issue, as I see it, is resolved, unless my learned friend has any further comment. Beyond that I don't think I can help you further unless there is another specific issue you would like me to address, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if Ms. Pilipovic has anything to add on this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I should just like in this connection to add a comment on my part. My learned friends and myself did agree on these 12 witnesses; however, in the assessment of the Defence, it would be a good thing if both parties could have agreement to work with all potential witnesses that occur in the materials of the Prosecution and the Defence, all the witnesses, not just these 12. This is something I have not discussed with my learned friends. As Mr. Mark Ierace is not present, I don't know whether the colleagues here present can take a position on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pilipovic, I would rather not discuss the question of witnesses now. What I am preoccupied with primarily is agreements on fact and law, or matters of dispute. After that, we can and should discuss witnesses. But in any event, I do acknowledge your concerns, and I have an understanding for your problems. But one must be logical. One must think about witnesses once we know that we have to prove such and such a fact. We cannot think about witnesses in the abstract. We talk about a witness because we need him to prove such and such a fact. If we are not agreed on the points of agreement and disagreement, then we can't move forward. That is the first thing we have to resolve, otherwise, we'll be turning around in a circle. So let me make a proposition to you. Ms. Pilipovic, have you anything to add? I'm sorry, maybe I cut you short.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with regard to facts which the parties need to agree on or which they disagree on, I have presented my position, and that is that after reviewing the material in the next two weeks I will be able to inform my learned friend which facts I can agree with and which I disagree with so that -- and our next meeting has been scheduled for the end of May which is a date that they have accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I think to go forward and to go more directly to the crux of the matter, I think we need to bear in mind a few points. The first is that tomorrow a new rule is coming into effect of Rule 65 ter which stipulates that we should do what we have already done in this case; that is, the participation of the legal officer in the preparation of a work plan decided by the pre-trial Judge. The second point is: I should like to know what is the view of the parties and their readiness to work together; that is, Mr. Ierace and Ms. Pilipovic, whether they're ready to work together to establish a schedule. And that is what I had intended to be done with the legal officer at our meeting of the 15th of March. We need such a timetable, and that timetable should be a part of the work plan. I have already told you that the objectives of that work plan are mentioned in Rule 65 ter, and I don't need to repeat it. That work plan will be one that will have the necessary methodology and conditions to achieve that goal. We have to count on the availability of persons, the availability of space, et cetera. A third idea to be kept in mind is that we may establish this work plan tomorrow or the day after, bearing in mind the information which the parties have provided today. So among these guidelines that I have just conveyed to you, there is a point I have to learn from you, and that is the availability and the readiness of the parties. Do we need to go into private session for that, or not? I don't think so, but tell me when Mr. Ierace will be available. I heard that you said this afternoon. And from Ms. Pilipovic, when she will be here so that we can work. I prefer to hear from you when you are available rather than to tell you in an authoritative way you have to be available on such and such a day, which is something I could do, but I should like to hear your views on this. Mr. Blaxill, have I understood correctly that Mr. Ierace is arriving today?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: He's certainly arriving today, Your Honour, but I believe his flight is schedule for about 10.00 this evening. I anticipate him being in the office tomorrow. And in fact I know he has appointments tomorrow, so yes, he should be here tomorrow. I don't know what his plans are obviously immediately for work load for the next few weeks, but I don't believe he's due on leave or out of the country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you very much, Mr. Blaxill. Ms. Pilipovic, what about your time, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm able to inform you that I am here today because I have been in The Hague for the past ten days. I'm leaving tomorrow morning. I can suggest that Mr. Ierace can contact me and inform me regarding dates, and then I can let him know whether they are suitable for me or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Perhaps you can contact Mr. Fourmy who is here in front of me because, as I have told you, we are going to prepare this work plan indicating the meetings with the help of the legal officer to implement that work plan. And I told you that the rule will come into effect tomorrow, but we have in fact already started implementing it. But we are going to apply that rule, and I think that we are going to tell you what this work plan will be, as well as the timetable. Regarding the timetable, perhaps it would be convenient to contact Mr. Fourmy to let him know when you are available, otherwise we will fix the dates. For the record, Mr. Fourmy, do you agree with this? Do you have any suggestions regarding the implementation of this new rule?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, no, at this stage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question: Madam Registrar, are there any problems regarding the formation of Ms. Pilipovic's team or is everything progressing well?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not aware of any problems, but I can speak with Christian Rohde and see if there's anything pending at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. I think we have taken stock of the situation. We have the guidelines for the future, so we have to embark upon our work in earnest. The hearing is adjourned for today until next time.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
